topic: Warehouse layer: dbt, DuckDB, dimensional modelling
why: FDEs are routinely the person a customer asks for 'just a weekly report' out of the product database, and the naive answer - a cron job running SELECTs against the OLTP primary - is what pages their DBA at 03:00 and produces numbers that disagree with the invoice. A tested, documented dbt + DuckDB mart is the smallest thing that gives you a stable grain, history that survives source overwrites, a reconciliation you can show the customer, and a project that ports to their Snowflake/BigQuery/Databricks by swapping the adapter when they outgrow one box. Dimensional-modelling vocabulary (grain, SCD2, conformed dimensions, additivity) is also the shared language with the customer's data team, and Palantir/Databricks-style loops test it directly.
prerequisites: SQL beyond SELECT: CTEs, window functions, multi-aggregate GROUP BY, joins with time-range predicates (Topic 29, PostgreSQL at depth)

DefenderMate's Postgres schema (tenants, users, conversations, messages, llm_calls, tool_calls, audit_log) and its RLS policies, because the extraction role must read across tenants (Topic 30, Data modelling for multi-tenant AI systems)
Python 3.11+ virtualenv hygiene and pinned requirements - dbt-core and dbt-duckdb are pip packages and version drift between them bites
YAML and Jinja2 basics: dbt projects are mostly YAML config and Jinja-templated SQL
Tests-as-assertions mindset from Topic 35 (Testing and contracts) - dbt tests are assertions over data, not code
Git branches plus a CI runner (GitHub Actions) for scheduling the nightly run and doing state-based builds

subtopics.name: When a warehouse layer is the right call, and when DuckDB is the right warehouse
subtopics.learn: Know the three reasons to stop reporting from the OLTP primary: row-store scan cost (Postgres reads whole 8 KB heap pages to aggregate three columns; a columnar engine reads only those columns and skips row groups via min/max zone maps), lock and IO contention with the production write path, and the need for history the application overwrites or deletes. Place DuckDB on the spectrum: in-process, single-node, vectorised, zero infrastructure, comfortable from gigabytes to low terabytes on one box; versus a Postgres read replica (no new tech but still row-store) versus Snowflake/BigQuery/Databricks (multi-user concurrency, governance, per-query cost). State the customer-facing rule you will use: start with DuckDB + Parquet + dbt when there is one consumer and the data fits on a disk, because the dbt project moves to a cloud warehouse later by changing profiles.yml, not by rewriting SQL.

subtopics.name: Kimball four-step design and declaring the grain
subtopics.learn: Apply the four steps to DefenderMate before writing a line of SQL: (1) pick the business process ('an LLM call was made', 'a conversation ran'), (2) declare the grain as a sentence - 'one row per llm_call', 'one row per tenant per day' - (3) identify dimensions as everything true at the moment of the event (tenant, user, model, date, tool), (4) identify facts as numeric measurements at that grain (input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_read_tokens, latency_ms, cost_usd). Recognise a mixed-grain fact table (conversation-level fields repeated on call-level rows) as the root cause of double counting in every downstream sum. Make the grain sentence the model's description: in YAML and enforce it with a unique test on the natural key or dbt_utils.unique_combination_of_columns, so a duplicated extract fails the build instead of inflating the email.

resource.label: Kimball Group - Four-Step Dimensional Design Process

subtopics.name: Fact table types and additivity: transaction, periodic snapshot, accumulating snapshot
subtopics.learn: Distinguish the three fact shapes and pick one per question: transaction facts (fct_llm_calls, one row per call, fully additive tokens and cost), periodic snapshots (fct_tenant_daily, one row per tenant per day whether or not anything happened - built by cross-joining a date spine to dim_tenant and zero-filling), and accumulating snapshots (one row per conversation with started_at, first_tool_call_at, resolved_at columns that get updated as milestones land). Classify every measure: additive (tokens, cost_usd), semi-additive (active_users - sums across tenants, not across days), non-additive (p95 latency, success ratio - never sum; store numerator and denominator, or recompute from the transaction grain). Understand why the weekly email must read the daily snapshot rather than re-aggregating transactions each time: stable, replayable numbers and explicit zero rows for silent tenants.

resource.label: Kimball Group - Periodic Snapshot Fact Tables

subtopics.name: Dimension design: surrogate keys, date dimension, conformed, role-playing, junk, degenerate, unknown member
subtopics.learn: Build dim_tenant, dim_user, dim_model, dim_date with a surrogate key (dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key over natural key plus dbt_valid_from for versioned rows), keep the natural key alongside it, and seed an 'unknown' member (-1 / 'unknown') so a fact row never loses its join when a lookup fails. Date dimension: generate with dbt_utils.date_spine, key it as a YYYYMMDD integer, include iso_week, week_start_date, is_weekend and any fiscal columns the email needs; role-play it as started_date and resolved_date by joining twice with aliases. Know when to fold low-cardinality flags (finish_reason x is_tool_call x is_cached) into a junk dimension and when to leave conversation_id on the fact as a degenerate dimension. Denormalise hierarchies (tenant -> plan -> region) into the dimension row rather than snowflaking; dimensions are small, so redundancy is cheaper than the extra join.

resource.label: Microsoft Learn - Modeling dimension tables (surrogate keys, SCD, special dimensions, date dimension)

subtopics.name: Slowly changing dimensions: Type 1 vs Type 2 with dbt snapshots
subtopics.learn: Decide per attribute whether a change is Type 1 (overwrite: user email, display name) or Type 2 (new version: tenant plan tier, model list price). Implement Type 2 with dbt snapshots: strategy: timestamp with updated_at when the source timestamp is trustworthy, strategy: check with check_cols when it is not; understand dbt_valid_from / dbt_valid_to (NULL means current), hard_deletes: invalidate | new_record (1.9+) and dbt_valid_to_current so you can avoid the NULL-handling branch in joins. Snapshots are append-only and cannot be regenerated from source - back the snapshot table up before any --full-refresh, and never snapshot an already-transformed or ephemeral model. Join facts to the version in effect at event time: f.created_at >= d.dbt_valid_from AND f.created_at < coalesce(d.dbt_valid_to, '9999-12-31'), and test that every fact row matches exactly one version.

resource.label: dbt docs - Add snapshots to your DAG

subtopics.name: Extracting from Postgres into DuckDB without hurting production
subtopics.learn: INSTALL postgres; LOAD postgres; ATTACH 'dbname=defendermate host=... user=reporting' AS pg (TYPE postgres, READ_ONLY); then CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE raw.llm_calls AS SELECT * FROM pg.public.llm_calls WHERE updated_at > (SELECT max(updated_at) FROM raw.llm_calls) - INTERVAL 1 HOUR. Use postgres_query('pg', '...') to push a filter to the server when the extension would otherwise pull the whole table; know that pg_use_ctid_scan and pg_pages_per_task parallelise the scan and what that does to the source's IO. Store credentials with CREATE SECRET (TYPE postgres, ...), not inline DSNs. Extraction hygiene an FDE is judged on: dedicated read-only role with statement_timeout, read from a replica when one exists, watermark on updated_at plus a lookback window for late-committing transactions, add an _extracted_at column, and reconcile nightly counts per day against the source. RLS from Topic 30 means the reporting role needs BYPASSRLS or a policy granting every tenant, otherwise the extract silently returns a subset.

resource.label: DuckDB docs - PostgreSQL extension (ATTACH, postgres_query, COPY, secrets)

subtopics.name: Parquet as the storage layer: COPY TO, hive partitioning, row groups, schema drift
subtopics.learn: Land raw extracts and published marts as Parquet: COPY (SELECT ...) TO 'lake/llm_calls' (FORMAT parquet, PARTITION_BY (event_date), COMPRESSION zstd, ROW_GROUP_SIZE 122880, OVERWRITE_OR_IGNORE). Read back with read_parquet('lake/llm_calls/*/*.parquet', hive_partitioning = true, union_by_name = true) and know partition pruning only happens when the WHERE clause is on the partition column. Sizing rules from the DuckDB performance guide: row groups of 100K-1M rows, files of 100 MB-10 GB, at least as many row groups as threads; per-tenant-per-hour partitions producing hundreds of thousands of tiny files is the classic mistake. Use parquet_metadata() and parquet_schema() to detect type drift between days (an INT64 column that became VARCHAR after an app deploy). Know dbt-duckdb's materialized='external' writes a model straight to Parquet using location and external_root from the profile.

resource.label: DuckDB docs - Reading and Writing Parquet Files

subtopics.name: dbt + dbt-duckdb project wiring: profiles.yml, dbt_project.yml, ref/source, compiled SQL
subtopics.learn: profiles.yml: type: duckdb, path: warehouse.duckdb, extensions: [parquet, httpfs, postgres], settings: {memory_limit: '8GB', threads: 4}, attach: for a second DuckDB file or Postgres; understand that threads at the profile top level is dbt's model-level parallelism, distinct from DuckDB's own threads setting. dbt_project.yml: model-paths, a models: block with per-folder +materialized and +schema, vars:, on-run-start / on-run-end, require-dbt-version. ref() and source() are what build the DAG - a hardcoded table name is an invisible dependency that will run out of order. Read target/compiled/ and target/run/ to see the exact SQL DuckDB executed; use dbt compile --select model when debugging Jinja; dbt debug verifies the profile and connection; dbt deps installs packages.yml.

subtopics.name: Layering: staging, intermediate, marts, and choosing a materialization per layer
subtopics.learn: Staging (stg_pg__llm_calls): one model per source table, view materialization, rename/cast/no joins, the only layer allowed to call source(). Intermediate (int_calls_with_costs): ephemeral or view, where joins and business rules live. Marts (fct_llm_calls, fct_tenant_daily, dim_tenant): table or incremental, the only layer consumers may query, landing in a marts schema via +schema. Decide materialization by asking: how often is it read versus how expensive is it to rebuild, does anyone query it directly, and how many rows. Understand that ephemeral models are injected as CTEs so compiled SQL balloons and error line numbers become useless - use views in dev and tables in prod by branching on target.name. Know why one model per source table matters: when the customer renames a column you fix one file.

resource.label: dbt docs - How we structure our dbt projects

subtopics.name: Incremental models: unique_key, strategies, lookback windows, late-arriving rows
subtopics.learn: {{ config(materialized='incremental', unique_key='llm_call_id', incremental_strategy='delete+insert', on_schema_change='append_new_columns') }} with {% if is_incremental() %} WHERE updated_at > (SELECT max(updated_at) FROM {{ this }}) - INTERVAL 1 HOUR {% endif %}. Know what each strategy does on a duplicate key (append duplicates, delete+insert replaces the key set, merge upserts) and which ones dbt-duckdb supports. The lookback window is what saves you from long-running source transactions that commit with older timestamps; on_schema_change defaults to ignore, which silently drops new source columns. dbt run --full-refresh rebuilds from scratch - guard expensive models with full_refresh: false. For fct_tenant_daily, key on (tenant_sk, date_day) and recompute the trailing N days each night rather than only yesterday so late events are absorbed. Late-arriving dimensions: coalesce a failed surrogate-key lookup to the unknown member and re-resolve within the lookback window.

subtopics.name: Jinja, macros and dbt_utils: surrogate keys, date spine, safe division, DRY logic
subtopics.learn: {{ }} renders a value, {% %} controls flow. Write a cents_to_usd(col) macro and a limit_in_dev() macro keyed on target.name. Use dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key(['tenant_id', 'dbt_valid_from']) for versioned dimension keys, dbt_utils.date_spine(datepart='day', start_date=..., end_date=...) to build dim_date and the snapshot spine, dbt_utils.safe_divide(successes, attempts) for tool-success ratios that must not divide by zero, and dbt_utils.star(from=ref(...), except=[...]) to avoid hand-listing columns. Pin packages.yml versions and understand dispatch picks the adapter-specific implementation. Jinja runs at compile time: {{ run_started_at }} is fixed for the whole invocation while current_timestamp is evaluated per statement, which matters when you stamp _loaded_at on multiple models.

subtopics.name: Data tests: generic, singular, thresholds and stored failures
subtopics.learn: Generic tests in YAML: unique and not_null on every key, accepted_values on finish_reason (end_turn, max_tokens, tool_use, stop_sequence), relationships so every fact tenant_sk exists in dim_tenant. dbt_utils tests that catch real regressions: unique_combination_of_columns (the grain), accepted_range (cost_usd >= 0, latency_ms between 0 and 600000), not_null_proportion, equal_rowcount between stg and raw, recency (mart refreshed within 26 hours). Singular tests in tests/*.sql for cross-model reconciliation: sum of fct_tenant_daily tokens per day must equal sum of fct_llm_calls tokens for that day. Configure severity: warn, warn_if: '>0', error_if: '>100' so a handful of bad rows does not block the email while a flood does; store_failures: true writes failing rows to <schema>_dbt_test__audit so you can show the customer the exact offending rows. Remember dbt build skips children of a failing test.

resource.label: dbt docs - Add data tests to your DAG

subtopics.name: Unit tests and model contracts: pinning logic and schema
subtopics.learn: Unit tests (dbt 1.8+) mock inputs and assert outputs: unit_tests: - name: prices_apply_cache_discount, model: int_calls_with_costs, given: [{input: ref('stg_pg__llm_calls'), rows: [...]}, {input: ref('dim_model'), rows: [...]}], expect: {rows: [...]}. Aim them at the pricing formula, UTC-vs-tenant-local day bucketing, and the SCD2 join-window predicate; use overrides to pin is_incremental() and vars. Model contracts: config: contract: enforced: true plus columns: - name: tenant_sk, data_type: bigint, constraints: [{type: not_null}] make the build fail when the SELECT's output schema drifts, which is what protects the email template from a renamed or retyped column. Contracts require every column listed with a data_type and are checked at build time before the table is swapped in.

subtopics.name: Source freshness and exposures: knowing the data is late, and who consumes it
subtopics.learn: Declare sources: with loaded_at_field: _extracted_at and freshness: warn_after: {count: 6, period: hour}, error_after: {count: 26, period: hour}; dbt source freshness writes target/sources.json and --select source_status:fresher+ builds only models whose sources actually moved. Add an exposures: entry (type: application, name: defendermate_weekly_email, owner:, url:, depends_on: [ref('fct_tenant_daily'), ref('dim_tenant')]) so the lineage graph ends at the customer email and dbt build --select +exposure:defendermate_weekly_email builds exactly that path. Treat the freshness thresholds as the mart's SLA contract with the customer and alert on them, not on 'the cron ran'.

resource.label: dbt docs - Add sources to your DAG (incl. source freshness)

subtopics.name: Documentation and lineage: descriptions, doc blocks, catalog and manifest
subtopics.learn: Every mart column gets a description:; define conformed definitions once as {% docs tenant_sk %}...{% enddocs %} blocks and reference them with '{{ doc("tenant_sk") }}' so the same column is not described three different ways. dbt docs generate writes catalog.json and manifest.json; dbt docs serve renders the searchable site and lineage DAG. Put the grain sentence, the freshness SLA and the owner in the model description rather than a wiki so they cannot drift from the code. Know manifest.json is machine-readable: it drives state:modified selection and you can turn it into a customer-facing data dictionary with a 30-line script.

subtopics.name: dbt build and node selection: tags, graph operators, state and result selectors
subtopics.learn: dbt build runs seeds, snapshots, models and tests in DAG order and skips descendants of failures. Selection syntax: --select tag:nightly, path:models/marts, stg_pg__llm_calls+ (downstream), +fct_tenant_daily (upstream), @fct_tenant_daily (children plus their parents), --exclude. State-based CI: keep the last production manifest.json and run dbt build --select state:modified+ --state prod-artifacts/ so a PR builds only what changed; after a partial failure rerun only the broken path with --select result:error+ --state target-prev/; --defer resolves unbuilt refs to production. Know --fail-fast to stop on first error and --empty for a schema-only dry run.

resource.label: dbt docs - Node selection syntax overview

subtopics.name: DuckDB analytical SQL for the mart: windows, QUALIFY, ASOF JOIN, PIVOT, list aggregates
subtopics.learn: Write the weekly-email queries idiomatically: lag(tokens, 7) OVER (PARTITION BY tenant_sk ORDER BY date_day) for week-over-week, sum(cost_usd) OVER (PARTITION BY tenant_sk ORDER BY date_day ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) for rolling 7-day, quantile_cont(latency_ms, 0.95) for p95, QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY tenant_id ORDER BY dbt_valid_from DESC) = 1 for current-version dedup without a subquery, ASOF JOIN dim_model_price p ON c.model = p.model AND c.created_at >= p.effective_from to attach the price in effect at call time, PIVOT fct_tenant_daily ON model_name USING sum(cost_usd), and list() / string_agg for the 'top 5 tools' line. Use GROUP BY ALL, SELECT * EXCLUDE (...), date_trunc('week', ...) and timezone(tz, ts) for tenant-local weeks. Confirm with EXPLAIN ANALYZE that filters push into the Parquet scan.

resource.label: DuckDB docs - Window Functions (incl. QUALIFY and frame clauses)

subtopics.name: DuckDB operability: memory limits, spilling, threads, single-writer concurrency, EXPLAIN ANALYZE
subtopics.learn: SET memory_limit = '6GB'; SET threads = 4; SET temp_directory = '/data/tmp'; SET max_temp_directory_size = '50GB'; SET preserve_insertion_order = false for large loads. Understand that hash joins, aggregates and sorts spill to temp_directory once memory_limit is hit, and that a missing or full temp directory is an OOM in disguise. Concurrency: one process may open a .duckdb file read-write; other processes may only attach with access_mode = 'READ_ONLY' and only if no writer holds it - so the nightly dbt job and the email renderer must not both open the same file read-write. Pattern: dbt writes warehouse.duckdb, then publish marts to Parquet or copy the file and atomically rename for readers. Threads within a process use MVCC and the second writer to the same row fails with a conflict error. Read EXPLAIN ANALYZE: estimated vs actual cardinality per operator, timings, and the accidental cross join that turns 4 minutes into 90.

subtopics.name: Nightly orchestration and the weekly-email consumer: scheduling, run_results.json, alerting, idempotency
subtopics.learn: A nightly run is: extract (DuckDB postgres ATTACH -> raw Parquet) -> dbt source freshness -> dbt build --select tag:nightly -> publish -> notify. Schedule with GitHub Actions on: schedule: cron: (know it runs on the default branch and can be delayed or dropped at high load) or a Temporal schedule from Topic 34 when you need retries and visibility; make every step idempotent so a 03:00 rerun is safe. Parse target/run_results.json: results[].status (success, error, fail, skipped, warn), failures, execution_time, adapter_response.rows_affected; post a summary to Slack and persist it to an ops.dbt_runs table via on-run-end. The weekly-email renderer (Python + Jinja2) opens the published DuckDB file with read_only=True or reads the Parquet marts, queries fct_tenant_daily for the trailing seven complete tenant-local days, and refuses to send when the recency test or freshness check failed - a late email beats a wrong one. Define the SLA explicitly: mart complete by 06:00 tenant-local, with freshness thresholds aligned to it.

resource.label: dbt docs - Run results JSON artifact

outcomes: You can write the grain of each fact table as a single sentence, encode it as a unique_combination_of_columns test, and demonstrate the build failing when a duplicated extract is loaded.

You can run dbt build on a fresh clone with only a Postgres DSN and end with fct_llm_calls, fct_tenant_daily, dim_tenant (SCD2), dim_model and dim_date materialised in DuckDB, every test passing, and dbt docs generate producing a lineage graph that terminates at the defendermate_weekly_email exposure.
You can change a tenant's plan tier in Postgres, run dbt snapshot, and show two versions in dim_tenant with correct dbt_valid_from/dbt_valid_to while historic calls remain attributed to the old tier.
You can insert an llm_call with a created_at three days in the past, rerun the incremental models without --full-refresh, and show the corrected fct_tenant_daily row for that day.

You can prove reconciliation to a customer: a singular test comparing per-day token sums between raw and fct_tenant_daily passes, and when it fails you can name the exact rows from the dbt_test__audit schema.
You can read EXPLAIN ANALYZE output on a query over hive-partitioned Parquet, state whether partition pruning and filter pushdown happened, and fix the layout or predicate so they do.
You can open run_results.json after a failed nightly run, identify the failed node and its skipped descendants, rerun only result:error+ with --state, and state whether the email is safe to send.

You can size DuckDB for a customer's box (memory_limit, threads, temp_directory), show a larger-than-memory aggregation completing by spilling, and explain the single-writer constraint to their ops team in two sentences.
failureModes: The reporting role extracted from a Postgres database with RLS enabled but had no BYPASSRLS and no policy; the extract silently returned rows for one tenant, not_null tests passed on the tiny table, and every other customer received a weekly email reporting zero usage.

An incremental fact filtered on created_at > max(created_at) with no lookback; a batch committed by a long-running transaction with older timestamps never landed, and weekly totals came in 4 percent below the invoice, which the customer noticed first.

Someone ran dbt snapshot --full-refresh on dim_tenant after adding a column, wiping version history; every historic fact then joined to the current plan tier and three months of reports silently changed.

Parquet partitioned by tenant_id and hour produced 400k files of a few kilobytes; DuckDB spent longer opening files than scanning them and the nightly run grew from 4 minutes to 90 before anyone looked.

The email renderer opened warehouse.duckdb with the default read-write mode while dbt was writing; the lock conflict surfaced on Monday morning as 'email service down' and was debugged as a networking problem for two hours.

on_schema_change was left at the default ignore, so a new cache_read_tokens column added upstream never reached fct_llm_calls; cost_usd omitted cache discounts for six weeks until the customer disputed the bill.

A refactor changed latency from milliseconds to seconds; the accepted_range test with max_value 600000 still passed and there was no contract pinning the unit, so p95 latency in the email read 0.8 for a month and nobody trusted the report afterward.
interviewQuestions: A customer wants a weekly usage-and-cost email per tenant from a Postgres OLTP database holding 200 million llm_call rows. Design the warehouse layer: which fact tables at which grain, which dimensions are SCD2, how you extract without hurting the primary, and what runs fine on a 16 GB box versus when you would move them to Snowflake or Databricks.

Explain the difference between a transaction fact and a periodic snapshot fact and why the weekly email should be built from the snapshot. What exactly goes wrong if you sum a p95 latency column across days, and how do you store it so the email is still right?

Your incremental model filters on updated_at > max(updated_at). Give me three concrete ways rows get lost or duplicated, and say which of unique_key, incremental strategy and a lookback window addresses each.

A tenant moved from 'pro' to 'enterprise' on March 3rd. Write the SQL that joins March calls to the plan in effect at call time using a dbt snapshot table, and tell me what breaks if dbt_valid_to is NULL for current rows and you forgot the coalesce.

dbt build failed at 03:14 on a relationships test between fct_llm_calls and dim_model. What do you look at in run_results.json and the stored-failures table, what are the two most likely root causes, and how do you decide whether the 07:00 customer email can still go out?

Why does DuckDB allow only one writer process, and how do you architect a nightly writer plus a daytime read service around that constraint? Separately, what is the difference between threads in profiles.yml and DuckDB's own threads setting?

A query over two years of hive-partitioned Parquet takes 40 seconds filtered on tenant_id but 400 milliseconds filtered on event_date. Explain why, and describe two different ways you would change the layout or the query so both are fast.
proofOfWork: A reproducible customer-handover package for the DefenderMate warehouse, checked into the repo alongside the dbt project: a single make nightly target that, from a fresh clone plus a Postgres DSN, extracts to Parquet via the DuckDB postgres extension, runs dbt source freshness and dbt build --select tag:nightly, publishes the marts, and appends the parsed run_results.json to an ops.dbt_runs table; a recorded drift drill in which you change a tenant's plan tier and insert a back-dated llm_call in Postgres, rerun the pipeline, and show dim_tenant with two versions, the corrected fct_tenant_daily row, the singular reconciliation test passing, and dbt docs lineage terminating at the weekly-email exposure; and a one-page ops runbook stating the mart SLA, the DuckDB memory_limit/threads/temp_directory settings for the customer's box, the single-writer constraint and how the email service avoids it, and the exact rerun command (dbt build --select result:error+ --state ...) after a partial failure. Finish with a rendered weekly email for one sample tenant generated from the mart, showing week-over-week token, cost and p95 deltas.
